title: A reason for hope (1 Peter 3:8–17)
hookLine: be ready to give a reason for your hope, with gentleness and respect
tomorrow: how do you open your door without the sigh?

cards: It comes over dinner, half curious, half skeptical: so why do you even believe all that? Then the table goes quiet, and every eye is on you. What do you say?

1 Peter saw that question coming, and wrote the answer's shape before the answer: "sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear."

teach.h: APOLOGIA: A REPLY, NOT A SORRY.
teach.b: Start with the word answer. In Greek it's apologia: not saying sorry, but a reply, the kind you give when someone asks you to account for yourself.
And the manner is part of the answer: meekness toward the one asking, and fear, here as reverence toward God. Today's line, gentleness and respect, is how newer English often puts those words.

Before all this, the passage sets the tone: "Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing." Railing means insult. So when the question comes sharp, the reply doesn't.
Now, how much should a Christian say? Christians hold two honest views.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: BE READY TO SPEAK.
teach.b: The first: speak up. Be ready always. A hope worth having is worth explaining, and people who hold this view study the reasons so they can give them plainly when asked.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: LET YOUR LIFE SPEAK.
teach.b: The second: let your life speak first. Earlier, the same letter hopes outsiders "may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God."

People who hold this view say a life that matches the hope is the answer, and words come when someone asks. Here's what both sides keep, the detail to tell a friend: the verse begins with being asked.
The answer is for the person who wants to know.

how: Some Christians study the reasons for their faith so they can answer questions, and others talk about faith mostly through how they live; 1 Peter 3:15 is quoted by both.

games.q: what does “a reason for hope” mean?
o: a debate you win by having more facts
a gentle answer for anyone who asks why you hope
a formal apology for something you did wrong

games.q: a reason for hope — tap the pairs.
p: good works, which they shall behold

s: 1 Peter tells Christians to argue people into believing
it says answer every man that asketh you, with meekness and fear.
apologia in 1 Peter means saying sorry
it means a reply, an account of yourself given when asked.
1 Peter says not to return insult for insult
not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing.

games.q: your cousin thinks Christians should keep faith quiet and just live well. you think it's good to explain when someone asks. what's the best case for HIS side?
o: 1 Peter says words about faith don't matter to God.
1 Peter hopes people see good works and glorify God.
1 Peter says never to talk about faith at all.
games.why: that's his view at its strongest: by your good works, which they shall behold (2:12). yours answers: be ready always to give an answer (3:15). both are Christian voices.

practice: Find one plain sentence for a hope you actually hold, about people, about tomorrow, or about God. Say it out loud, softly, the way you'd say it to someone who disagrees and whom you respect. Then let the rest of the sit be quiet.

orig.note: Greek: an answer, a reasoned reply. 1 Peter 3:15, ready always to give an answer.

carryVoice: The line to keep: gentleness and respect, the answer and the manner both. Talk tomorrow.
